paper_title: Breaking Bias, Building Bridges Evaluation and Mitigation of Social   Biases in LLMs via Contact Hypothesis
caption: Lighter shaded bars show the percentage of prompts that generate biased responses before instruction tuning, whereas darker shaded bars correspond to the same after instruction tuning. Darker bars begin at the top of the lighter bars (for example, for the first bar, the lighter bar is 39.50%, and the darker bar is only 0.04%). Takeaway: Instruction-tuning on certain key principles eliminates bias to nearly zero (visualized by the absence of dark bars) across prompts specific to Support of Authorities and Extended Contact, also considerably reducing bias across Virtual Contact prompts.
model_annotation: The bar chart illustrates the effectiveness of instruction tuning in reducing social bias across three contact-based prompt categories—“Support of Authorities,” “Extended Contact,” and “Virtual Contact”—as evaluated in the study “Breaking Bias, Building Bridges.” The vertical axis represents “Bias Percentage,” ranging from 0 to 70, while the horizontal axis lists the three prompt categories. Each category contains three grouped bars, representing “No Contact Before/After,” “Positive Contact Before/After,” and “Negative Contact Before/After,” with lighter shades indicating bias percentages before instruction tuning and darker shades showing the incremental bias added after tuning (stacked on top). For “Support of Authorities,” bias before tuning is 39.50% (No Contact), 31.83% (Positive Contact), and 42.38% (Negative Contact), with post-tuning additions of only 0.04%, 0.00%, and 0.00%, respectively—effectively eliminating bias. Similarly, “Extended Contact” shows pre-tuning biases of 40.61%, 36.13%, and 47.28%, with post-tuning additions of 0.00%, 0.00%, and 0.11%, again indicating near-total bias removal. In “Virtual Contact,” pre-tuning biases are 39.74%, 39.17%, and 43.83%, with post-tuning additions of 10.00%, 10.01%, and 10.02%, showing a significant but incomplete reduction. The chart visually emphasizes that instruction tuning nearly eradicates bias in the first two categories, while substantially mitigating it in the third, supporting the paper’s claim that targeted instruction can effectively reduce social bias in LLMs via the contact hypothesis framework.
